requirements: The core contributions of FlashAttention-2 — reduced non-matmul FLOPs, sequence-length parallelism, and improved warp partitioning — have been reproduced end-to-end, matching the paper's attention microbenchmarks and GPT-style training throughput.

sub_tasks.requirements: The reproduction environment (A100 80GB SXM4 for microbenchmarks and end-to-end training, optional H100 80GB SXM5 for the H100 benchmarks) is provisioned with the correct CUDA/PyTorch/xformers/Triton stack needed to build FlashAttention-2 and run all baselines.
GPU hardware matching the paper's benchmark hosts is available and detected by the reproduction scripts.

Code has been implemented that queries the local GPU (via `nvidia-smi` or `torch.cuda.get_device_properties`) and verifies at least one NVIDIA A100 80GB SXM4 device (compute capability 8.0, ~80 GB HBM) is present before launching any Section 4.1 microbenchmark; the check fails loudly if the device is missing or has less than 80 GB memory.

Code has been implemented that optionally detects an NVIDIA H100 80GB SXM5 (compute capability 9.0) and gates the Figure-7 H100 benchmarks on its presence, skipping them cleanly with a documented reason when only A100s are available.

Code has been implemented that verifies 8×A100 80GB SXM GPUs (single node) are visible to the process for the Table 1 end-to-end GPT training runs; the check reports the discovered device count and fails with a clear message if fewer than 8 devices are present.
CUDA toolkit and low-level build dependencies required to compile the FlashAttention-2 CUDA/CUTLASS kernels are installed and functional.

Code has been implemented that verifies a CUDA toolkit (nvcc) of version ≥11.6 is installed and that `nvcc --version` runs successfully; this version is the minimum supported by the FlashAttention-2 build.

Code has been implemented that installs the C++/CUDA build prerequisites (ninja, packaging, wheel, a C++17 compiler such as g++≥9) needed to build the flash-attn extension from source without falling back to a slow non-ninja build.
The Python deep-learning stack (PyTorch, Triton, xformers) required to run every attention implementation compared in Section 4 is installed with matching CUDA support.

Code has been implemented that installs PyTorch (≥2.0) built against the same CUDA major version as the local toolkit and verifies `torch.cuda.is_available()` is True and `torch.version.cuda` matches the installed nvcc.

Code has been implemented that installs the Triton package (version compatible with the reference `openai/triton` `06-fused-attention.py` tutorial cited by the paper) and confirms `import triton` succeeds; this is required to benchmark the Triton FlashAttention baseline.

Code has been implemented that installs the `xformers` library including its CUTLASS-based memory-efficient attention op and verifies `xformers.ops.memory_efficient_attention` is importable; this provides the "xformers (cutlass)" baseline shown in Figures 4–6.
Both FlashAttention v1 (baseline) and FlashAttention-2 (this paper) are built and importable so the two can be benchmarked side by side.

Code has been implemented that builds and installs the FlashAttention-2 package (from the `Dao-AILab/flash-attention` source in this repo or a pinned v2.x release) targeting the local GPU's compute capability, and confirms `from flash_attn import flash_attn_func` succeeds after install.

Code has been implemented that also makes the original FlashAttention v1 kernel available (either via a pinned v1.x wheel or via the v1-compatible entry points shipped inside FlashAttention-2) so that the "FlashAttention" baseline curves in Figures 4–7 can actually be executed against the same tensors as FlashAttention-2.
The environment is captured in a reproducible form and its correctness is smoke-tested before any benchmark or training run.

A `requirements.txt`, `environment.yml`, `pyproject.toml`, or equivalent pinned manifest is written that lists exact versions of torch, triton, xformers, flash-attn, ninja, and CUDA toolkit, and `reproduce.sh` invokes it (or a build script) to recreate the environment from a clean base image.

Code has been implemented that runs an end-to-end environment smoke test (a tiny FP16 `flash_attn_func` call on a Q/K/V of shape (1, 128, 4, 64), plus one call each of the PyTorch, xformers, and Triton baselines on the same inputs) and asserts all four produce finite outputs within a small tolerance of one another before any Section 4 benchmark begins.

Baseline attention implementations used in the benchmarks are available and callable through a unified harness: a standard PyTorch attention (materializing S and P per Section 2.2), FlashAttention v1 (original CUDA kernel), FlashAttention in xformers (the `cutlass` memory_efficient_attention op), and FlashAttention in Triton (openai/triton `python/tutorials/06-fused-attention.py`, referenced in footnote 3).
A standard PyTorch attention baseline (as described in Section 2.2) is available, materializing S=QK^T and P=softmax(S) to memory and computing O=PV.

Code has been implemented that defines a standard PyTorch attention function (e.g., `pytorch_attention(q, k, v, causal=False)`) which explicitly forms S = Q @ K^T / sqrt(d), applies optional causal mask, computes P = softmax(S), and returns O = P @ V using standard torch ops (no fused kernel).

Code has been implemented such that the PyTorch attention baseline, run on random FP16 (Q,K,V) with N=1024, d=64, produces outputs that match a reference torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention call within an absolute tolerance ≤1e-2 (FP16 numerical parity).

Code has been implemented such that the PyTorch attention baseline supports both `causal=True` (applying an upper-triangular −inf mask to S before softmax) and `causal=False`, and both head dimensions d=64 and d=128 used in the Section 4.1 sweep.
The original FlashAttention (v1) CUDA kernel baseline is installed and callable.

Code has been implemented and environment set up so that a released version of the original FlashAttention package (`flash_attn`, e.g. a v1.x tag prior to FlashAttention-2, exposing the original CUDA kernel) is installed and importable in the reproduction environment.

Code has been implemented that wraps the FlashAttention-v1 CUDA kernel (e.g. `flash_attn.flash_attn_func` or the equivalent v1 entrypoint) behind the same `(q, k, v, causal)` signature used by the other baselines in the benchmark harness, invoking the CUDA path (not the Triton or xformers path).

Code has been implemented such that the FlashAttention-v1 baseline, run forward+backward with random FP16 inputs (N=1024, d=64, causal=False), produces outputs and gradients dQ,dK,dV that agree with the standard PyTorch baseline within absolute tolerance ≤1e-2.
The xformers `cutlass` FlashAttention baseline is installed and callable.

Code has been implemented and environment set up so that the `xformers` library is installed with the `cutlass` FlashAttention op available (importable as `xformers.ops.fmha.cutlass.FwOp`/`BwOp` or callable via `xformers.ops.memory_efficient_attention(..., op=(cutlass_fw, cutlass_bw))`).

Code has been implemented that wraps `xformers.ops.memory_efficient_attention` with an explicit `op=` selection forcing the `cutlass` FlashAttention path (not the flash/triton fallbacks), exposed behind the same `(q, k, v, causal)` signature used by the harness, and using `LowerTriangularMask` when `causal=True`.

Code has been implemented such that the xformers-cutlass baseline forward+backward output and gradients on random FP16 inputs (N=1024, d=64) match the PyTorch baseline within absolute tolerance ≤1e-2 both with and without causal masking.
The FlashAttention in Triton baseline is available, sourced from openai/triton `python/tutorials/06-fused-attention.py` (footnote 3).

Code has been implemented that vendors or fetches the openai/triton `06-fused-attention.py` tutorial (the Phil Tillet Triton FlashAttention implementation referenced in footnote 3) into the repository at a fixed pinned commit compatible with the installed `triton` version.

Code has been implemented that exposes the Triton `attention` function from `06-fused-attention.py` behind the harness's uniform `(q, k, v, causal)` signature and successfully runs a forward and a backward pass on FP16 inputs of shape (batch, nheads, N, d) = (2, 16, 1024, 64) without raising.

Code has been implemented such that the Triton FlashAttention baseline forward+backward output and gradients on random FP16 inputs (N=1024, d=64) match the PyTorch baseline within absolute tolerance ≤1e-2 for both causal and non-causal settings.

A unified benchmarking harness dispatches all four baselines (PyTorch, FlashAttention CUDA, xformers-cutlass, Triton) under the Section 4.1 setting and reports TFLOPs/s using the paper's FLOP formulas.

Code has been implemented that provides a single benchmark driver accepting a baseline name from {`pytorch`, `flash`, `xformers_cutlass`, `triton`} plus `(batch, seqlen, nheads, headdim, causal)` and runs a warmup + timed loop (using `torch.cuda.Event` or `triton.testing.do_bench`) returning median wall-clock time per iteration.

Code has been implemented such that the harness computes forward-pass FLOPs as 4 · batch · nheads · seqlen^2 · headdim (matching the paper's Section 4.1 formula), backward-pass FLOPs as 2.5 × forward FLOPs, and divides by 2 when `causal=True`, then converts (FLOPs / seconds) to TFLOPs/s.

Code has been implemented such that the harness sweeps sequence length ∈ {512, 1024, 2048, 4096, 8192, 16384} with batch chosen so total tokens = 16384, hidden dim = 2048, and headdim ∈ {64, 128} (nheads = 32 or 16), matching the Section 4.1 benchmark setting, and handles per-baseline OOM by recording an `OOM` entry rather than crashing the sweep.

Algorithm 1 (FlashAttention-2 forward pass) is implemented as specified, including the reduced-rescale online-softmax tweak (maintain un-scaled O and only divide by ℓ at the end) and storing the logsumexp L instead of the (m, ℓ) pair.
The forward-pass kernel exposes the correct external interface, block partitioning, and HBM tensors described in Algorithm 1 (lines 1–2).

Code has been implemented that defines a FlashAttention-2 forward-pass entry point (e.g., a Python/PyTorch autograd function or a CUDA/Triton kernel launch wrapper) taking Q, K, V tensors of shape (N, d) or (batch, heads, N, d) and returning both the output O of the same shape and a logsumexp tensor L of shape (..., N).

Code has been implemented so that the forward-pass entry point accepts configurable row and column block sizes Br and Bc (either as arguments or as compile-time constants selected per head dimension), and the block sizes actually used at runtime fall within the {64,128} × {64,128} set discussed in the paper.

The implementation partitions Q into Tr = ceil(N/Br) row blocks of size Br × d, and K and V into Tc = ceil(N/Bc) column blocks of size Bc × d, correctly handling the case where N is not divisible by Br or Bc (e.g., via masking of padding rows/columns).

The implementation allocates a logsumexp buffer L of size N (per batch and per head) in HBM and writes into it per row block, matching the split of L into Tr blocks of size Br described on line 2 of Algorithm 1.
The outer loop over row blocks (lines 3–5) loads Q_i to SRAM and initializes per-row-block accumulators with the values specified in Algorithm 1.

Code has been implemented that iterates i from 1 to Tr (mapping each row block to a thread block or an equivalent parallel worker), and inside the body first loads the Q_i tile of shape Br × d from HBM into on-chip storage before entering the inner loop.

Code has been implemented that, at the start of each outer-loop iteration, initializes the on-chip accumulators to O_i^{(0)} = zeros(Br, d), ℓ_i^{(0)} = zeros(Br), and m_i^{(0)} = full(Br, -inf), exactly as in line 5 of Algorithm 1.
The inner loop over K/V blocks (lines 6–11) implements S = QK^T, the online rowmax/exp/rowsum recursions, and the un-scaled O update exactly as specified.

Code has been implemented that, for each inner-loop index j from 1 to Tc, loads the corresponding K_j and V_j tiles (each of shape Bc × d) from HBM into on-chip storage before performing the tile matmuls.

Code has been implemented that computes the score tile S_i^{(j)} = Q_i · K_j^T of shape Br × Bc using an on-chip matmul (e.g., a Tensor Core / MMA op), including the 1/sqrt(d) scaling of QK^T that the paper omits for clarity but is required for standard attention.
Code has been implemented that updates the running row-max as m_i^{(j)} = max(m_i^{(j-1)}, rowmax(S_i^{(j)})) elementwise across the Br rows of the tile.
Code has been implemented that produces the unnormalized probability tile P̃_i^{(j)} = exp(S_i^{(j)} − m_i^{(j)}) via pointwise subtraction of the per-row current max followed by exponentiation.

Code has been implemented that updates the running row-sum-of-exponentials as ℓ_i^{(j)} = exp(m_i^{(j-1)} − m_i^{(j)}) * ℓ_i^{(j-1)} + rowsum(P̃_i^{(j)}), applying the correction factor before adding the current-tile rowsum.

Code has been implemented that updates the output accumulator as O_i^{(j)} = diag(exp(m_i^{(j-1)} − m_i^{(j)})) · O_i^{(j-1)} + P̃_i^{(j)} · V_j, using the per-row exponential correction on the previous O and the on-chip matmul of P̃ with V_j.
The two non-matmul-reducing tweaks introduced in Section 3.1.1 are implemented: the un-scaled O accumulator (no per-block 1/ℓ division) and storing L = m + log(ℓ) instead of the (m, ℓ) pair.

The inner-loop body must NOT divide the O accumulator by ℓ_i^{(j)} at any per-iteration step (i.e., the FlashAttention-1 diag(ℓ^{(j)})^{-1} factor that appeared inside the loop must be absent), so that O_i^{(j)} remains an un-scaled sum of P̃V terms.

Code has been implemented that, exactly once after the inner loop completes, rescales the accumulator as O_i = diag(ℓ_i^{(Tc)})^{-1} · O_i^{(Tc)} (line 12 of Algorithm 1) — this is the only place ℓ is applied to O.

Code has been implemented that computes L_i = m_i^{(Tc)} + log(ℓ_i^{(Tc)}) once per row block after the inner loop (line 13 of Algorithm 1), and only L is exposed as the auxiliary output — the raw (m, ℓ) pair is not persisted to HBM for the backward pass.
The saved auxiliary tensor L has shape (..., N) (one scalar per query row, matching the row-wise logsumexp), and no additional (..., N) tensor for the row-max m is written to HBM alongside it.
The finalization and HBM write-back (lines 14–17) correctly emit the i-th block of O and the i-th block of L and return the pair (O, L).
Code has been implemented that writes the finalized O_i tile back to HBM at rows [i*Br : (i+1)*Br] of the output tensor O.
Code has been implemented that writes the per-row logsumexp vector L_i (length Br) back to HBM at positions [i*Br : (i+1)*Br] of the L tensor.
The entry point returns the pair (O, L) (or an equivalent named tuple / autograd-context save) so that the backward pass can consume L directly, as required by Algorithm 2's Require: line.
Behavioral and numerical correctness of the forward pass on unit-scale inputs against a reference softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d))V implementation.

A deterministic unit test exists that generates small Q, K, V (e.g., N=128, d=64, FP16) and asserts that the O returned by the FlashAttention-2 forward pass agrees with a naive PyTorch reference O_ref = softmax(Q @ K^T / sqrt(d), dim=-1) @ V within max absolute error 5e-3 and mean absolute error 5e-4.

A deterministic unit test exists that asserts the returned L agrees with the reference row-wise logsumexp L_ref = logsumexp(Q @ K^T / sqrt(d), dim=-1) within max absolute error 1e-2 (FP16 inputs, FP32 accumulators).

A deterministic unit test exists that runs the forward pass with adversarially large-magnitude scores (e.g., Q, K scaled by 100 so raw S has entries in the thousands) and confirms O is still finite and matches the reference within the same tolerance — verifying that the running-max subtraction inside the online softmax prevents overflow.

A deterministic unit test exists that runs the forward pass for head dimensions d ∈ {64, 128} and sequence lengths N ∈ {512, 1024, 2048}, in both non-causal and causal modes, and confirms the output matches the reference within tolerance for every configuration.

A behavioral test exists that measures the peak additional GPU memory allocated by the forward pass (beyond the Q, K, V, O tensors) and confirms it grows as O(N) — specifically, doubling N should at most roughly double the extra allocation, not quadruple it — verifying the O(N) memory claim of Section 3.1.1.

A behavioral test exists that counts (via a Python instrumentation of the reference-mode path, or a static analysis of the CUDA/Triton source) the number of per-inner-iteration division operations applied to the O accumulator, and confirms it is 0 for the FlashAttention-2 implementation (vs. 1 for a FlashAttention-1 reference), demonstrating the reduced non-matmul FLOPs tweak.
Algorithm 2 (FlashAttention-2 backward pass) is implemented as specified, including the softmax recomputation via logsumexp L, computation of D = rowsum(dO ∘ O), and correct dQ/dK/dV block updates.
The backward-pass kernel exposes an API and block partitioning consistent with Algorithm 2's Require and setup lines (steps 1–3).
Code has been implemented that exposes a backward-pass entry point accepting Q, K, V, O, dO ∈ R^{N×d} and the logsumexp vector L ∈ R^N (all in HBM) plus block sizes Bc, Br, and returning dQ, dK, dV.
Code has been implemented that partitions Q into Tr = ceil(N/Br) row blocks Q_1,...,Q_Tr of size Br × d.
Code has been implemented that partitions K and V into Tc = ceil(N/Bc) column blocks each of size Bc × d.
Code has been implemented that partitions O and dO into Tr row blocks of size Br × d each, matching the Q partitioning.
Code has been implemented that partitions L into Tr blocks L_1,...,L_Tr of size Br each, aligned with the Q/O row blocks.
Code has been implemented that initializes dQ ∈ R^{N×d} to zero in HBM partitioned into Tr row blocks, and dK, dV ∈ R^{N×d} partitioned into Tc column blocks of size Bc × d each.
Line 4 of Algorithm 2 is implemented: the row-wise D = rowsum(dO ∘ O) vector is precomputed and partitioned before the main loops.
Code has been implemented that computes D_i = row-wise sum of the elementwise product (dO ∘ O), yielding a vector of length N.
Code has been implemented that writes D to HBM and partitions it into Tr blocks D_1,...,D_Tr of size Br each, available for the inner loop's dS computation.
A unit test verifies that the computed D vector matches torch.sum(dO * O, dim=-1) elementwise within FP16 tolerance for random Q, K, V, dO.
The nested loop structure of Algorithm 2 (outer loop over column blocks j, inner loop over row blocks i) is implemented with correct load/init/write sequencing.
Code has been implemented so that the outer loop iterates j from 1 to Tc, loading K_j and V_j from HBM to on-chip SRAM once per outer iteration (line 6).
Code has been implemented so that on entry to each outer iteration, dK_j and dV_j are initialized to zero of shape Bc × d on SRAM (line 7).
Code has been implemented so that the inner loop iterates i from 1 to Tr and loads Q_i, O_i, dO_i, dQ_i, L_i, D_i from HBM to on-chip SRAM at each iteration (line 9).
Code has been implemented that, after the inner loop completes for a given j, writes the accumulated dK_j and dV_j from SRAM back to HBM (line 18).
The per-block gradient computations inside the inner loop (lines 10–16 of Algorithm 2) are implemented, including softmax recomputation from L and each dV/dP/dS/dQ/dK update.
The softmax matrix P_i^(j) is recomputed on-chip from the logsumexp L_i alone (no separately stored row-max m or row-sum ℓ) as specified in Section 3.1.2.
Code has been implemented that computes S_i^(j) = Q_i K_j^T on chip producing a Br × Bc tile (line 10).
Code has been implemented that computes P_i^(j) = exp(S_ij − L_i) on chip using only the logsumexp vector L_i (line 11), with L_i broadcast row-wise.
A unit test verifies that P reconstructed from S and L equals torch.softmax(S, dim=-1) within FP16 tolerance on random inputs.
Code has been implemented that accumulates dV_j ← dV_j + (P_i^(j))^T dO_i on-chip inside the inner loop (line 12).
Code has been implemented that computes dP_i^(j) = dO_i V_j^T on-chip producing a Br × Bc tile (line 13).
Code has been implemented that computes the softmax gradient dS_i^(j) = P_i^(j) ∘ (dP_i^(j) − D_i) on-chip, with D_i broadcast row-wise (line 14).

Code has been implemented for the dQ update: dQ_i is loaded from HBM into SRAM, updated on-chip as dQ_i ← dQ_i + dS_i^(j) K_j, and written back to HBM (line 15); the update is safe under sequence-length parallelism (e.g. atomic add or serial per-i sequencing).
Code has been implemented that accumulates dK_j ← dK_j + (dS_i^(j))^T Q_i on-chip inside the inner loop (line 16).
The end-to-end backward pass returns dQ, dK, dV that match a reference PyTorch autograd implementation of attention within FP16 numerical tolerance across representative configurations.

A test verifies that the backward-pass dQ output matches torch.autograd.grad on a reference standard-attention implementation within max-abs error ≤ 5e-3 in FP16 for N=1024, d=64, batch=2, heads=4 on random inputs.
A test verifies that the backward-pass dK output matches the reference torch autograd gradient within max-abs error ≤ 5e-3 in FP16 for the same configuration.
A test verifies that the backward-pass dV output matches the reference torch autograd gradient within max-abs error ≤ 5e-3 in FP16 for the same configuration.
A test verifies numerical correctness of dQ, dK, dV against a causally-masked reference autograd (upper-triangular S masked to −∞) within max-abs error ≤ 5e-3 in FP16.
Numerical correctness of dQ, dK, dV is verified for both head dimensions 64 and 128 (the two settings benchmarked in Section 4.1), each within max-abs error ≤ 5e-3 vs. reference.

The backward algorithm's asymptotic FLOPs, matmul count, and additional-memory footprint match the specification (5 matmuls per block pair, O(N^2 d) FLOPs, O(N) additional memory beyond inputs/outputs).

The inner loop executes exactly the 5 matmuls described in Section 2.3.2 (S = QK^T, dV += P^T dO, dP = dO V^T, dQ += dS K, dK += dS^T Q) per (i,j) block pair, verifiable by reading the kernel source or a matmul-call counter test.

The backward pass's total FLOP count scales as O(N^2 d) and equals roughly 2.5× the forward-pass FLOPs when measured (or documented) on a fixed configuration, matching the paper's Section 4.1 accounting.

Additional HBM allocated by the backward pass beyond Q, K, V, O, dO, dQ, dK, dV, L is O(N) (only D and small workspaces), and no N×N tensor is materialized; a test confirms peak extra memory grows linearly (not quadratically) with sequence length.

The causal-mask block-skipping optimization is implemented: blocks whose column indices all exceed row indices are skipped entirely, and masking is only applied to the single diagonal block per row, yielding the paper's ~1.7-1.8× speedup relative to non-causal attention on comparable shapes.
Block-level position classification is implemented so the causal-mask logic can distinguish fully-masked, diagonal, and fully-unmasked blocks per (row-block i, column-block j) pair.

Code has been implemented in the FlashAttention-2 forward kernel that, for every (i, j) block pair, computes whether the block lies strictly above the diagonal (j*Bc >= (i+1)*Br), on the diagonal (j*Bc < (i+1)*Br and (j+1)*Bc > i*Br), or strictly below the diagonal (using Br, Bc row/column block sizes and start offsets).

For a range of (Br, Bc, i, j) inputs including a strictly upper-triangular block, a diagonal block, and a strictly lower-triangular block, the classification helper returns the expected 'skip', 'mask', or 'no-mask' label so the kernel dispatches to the correct path.

For causal mode, the inner column-block loop over j is bounded so it only iterates up to the diagonal block for each row-block i (e.g., j <= min(Tc-1, ((i+1)*Br - 1) // Bc)) rather than iterating all Tc blocks, avoiding launching work for provably-masked columns.
Blocks whose column indices all strictly exceed the row indices of the row-block are skipped entirely: no S=QK^T matmul, no exp/rowmax/rowsum, and no update to the running (m, ℓ, O) statistics.

Code has been implemented so that when the (i, j) block is classified as strictly upper-triangular under the causal mask, the kernel does not perform the QK^T matmul, the softmax rescaling, or the P V matmul for that block.

A unit test drives the kernel (or its Python reference) with an input configuration where several trailing column blocks are strictly upper-triangular and verifies via an instrumented counter (or by comparing against an execution that iterates every block) that no matmul or exp op is performed for those skipped blocks.

The running per-row statistics m_i, ℓ_i, and O_i remain unchanged across iterations of the inner loop that correspond to skipped blocks (verified by asserting equality of these tensors before and after the skipped-block iteration in a unit test).

The causal mask itself (setting entries with j > i to -inf before softmax) is only applied on the single diagonal block per row-block; blocks strictly below the diagonal skip the mask-application code path entirely.

Code has been implemented so that when the (i, j) block is classified as the diagonal block, the kernel constructs the boolean mask (row_idx[:, None] >= col_idx[None, :]) and sets S entries failing this predicate to -inf before the exp step.

For (i, j) blocks classified as strictly lower-triangular (all row indices strictly greater than all column indices), the kernel executes the S=QK^T and P V matmuls without any mask construction or elementwise -inf write, verified either by branch instrumentation or by an equivalence test against an unmasked reference for these blocks.

On a small handcrafted example whose sequence length equals two row-blocks, the values produced by the diagonal-block mask path match an explicit reference in which the entire causal mask is applied densely to S (bitwise-equal in FP64, close in FP16/BF16 within numerical tolerance).
End-to-end numerical correctness of causal FlashAttention-2 is preserved by the block-skipping and diagonal-only-mask optimizations.

Code has been implemented that compares the causal FlashAttention-2 forward output against a naive reference softmax(QK^T + causal_mask)V over sequence lengths {512, 1024, 2048}, head dimensions {64, 128}, and both FP16 and BF16, asserting max absolute error within the same tolerance used for the non-causal path (e.g., <= 3x the reference-vs-FP32 error).
The paper's claim that block-skipping under the causal mask yields ~1.7-1.8× speedup vs. attention without a causal mask on comparable shapes is empirically reproduced.

Code has been implemented that benchmarks FlashAttention-2 forward+backward runtime with causal=True and causal=False at matched (batch, heads, seqlen, head_dim) configurations (varying seqlen over {2k, 4k, 8k, 16k}, head_dim in {64, 128}) on the same GPU, and computes the ratio runtime(non-causal) / runtime(causal).

At the largest measured sequence length (>= 8k tokens) with head dimension 128 on an A100 80GB SXM4, the measured runtime(non-causal) / runtime(causal) ratio for FlashAttention-2 forward+backward falls within the paper's stated ~1.7-1.8× range (accept values in approximately [1.5, 2.0] to allow benchmarking noise), demonstrating the block-skip speedup.

Multi-query attention (MQA) and grouped-query attention (GQA) are supported by index manipulation rather than key/value duplication, and the backward pass correctly sums dK/dV across implicitly duplicated heads.
The public attention entry point exposes MQA/GQA configuration by accepting Q with a different number of heads than K/V and validating the grouping ratio.

Code has been implemented so that the FlashAttention-2 forward and backward Python API accept Q of shape (..., num_heads_q, ..., d) together with K, V of shape (..., num_heads_kv, ..., d) where num_heads_q may be greater than num_heads_kv (in particular num_heads_kv = 1 for MQA and num_heads_kv > 1 dividing num_heads_q for GQA).

Code has been implemented so that the API raises (or otherwise clearly rejects) any call in which num_heads_q is not an integer multiple of num_heads_kv, and accepts the canonical special cases num_heads_kv == num_heads_q (MHA), num_heads_kv == 1 (MQA), and 1 < num_heads_kv < num_heads_q with num_heads_q % num_heads_kv == 0 (GQA).
The forward pass supports MQA/GQA by indexing into shared K/V heads rather than materializing duplicated K/V heads in memory.

Code has been implemented so that the forward kernel/dispatcher computes the K/V head index for a given query head via a group-mapping (kv_head_index = query_head_index // (num_heads_q / num_heads_kv)) and loads K_j, V_j from the shared K/V tensor using that index, without calling any tensor expand/repeat/tile that physically replicates K or V along the head dimension before the kernel.

Code has been implemented so that a runtime check confirms MQA/GQA does not materialize duplicated K/V: for a configuration with num_heads_q = 32, num_heads_kv = 1 (or 4), sequence length 2048, d_head = 64, the peak K/V-tensor memory allocated for the attention call scales with num_heads_kv (not num_heads_q), matching the un-duplicated shape to within measurement noise.

The FlashAttention-2 MQA forward output (num_heads_q = 16, num_heads_kv = 1, N = 2048, d = 64, fp16) matches, elementwise, a reference computation obtained by torch.repeat_interleave-ing K and V along the head dim to 16 heads and running the standard MHA forward, to within max abs error <= 5e-3 and mean abs error <= 5e-4.
